# Analysis of K-12 teachers’ demand characteristics for digital educational resource services from the perspective of adaptive feedback: based on the analysis of KANO model

**Rui Feng**<strong><sup>1</sup></strong> **· Jianghua Luo**<a href="http://orcid.org/0009-0008-9716-8091"><strong><sup>1</sup></strong></a>

Received: 14 April 2024 / Accepted: 8 August 2024 / Published online: 2 September 2024 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2024

## Abstract

Based on the adaptive feedback theory, promoting the development of digital educational resource services towards adaptability is key to solving the problem of poor applicability in current K-12 digital educational resource services. Demanddriven resource service construction plays a significant guiding role in this process, making it essential to clarify the demands of K-12 teachers for resource services. Therefore, this study employed a combination of large-scale interviews and Kano model analysis to summarize the composition, categories, and characteristics of teachers’ demands, based on the analysis of resource service elements. The research findings reveal that teachers expect resource services to provide convenient, personalized, and continuously evolving support for teaching, professional development, and students’ self-regulated learning scenarios. In terms of prioritizing these demands, teachers believe that addressing the demands in teaching scenario should take precedence before expanding to other scenarios. Finally, based on these research findings, a three-stage construction strategy has been designed: first, focusing on services for teaching scenario; second, addressing professional development and services for self-regulated learning; third, continuously improving the services. This strategy aims to enhance service quality and efficiency, providing guidance for the development of digital educational resource services in K-12 education.

**Keywords** Adaptive feedback · Digital educational resource services · Kano model · Demand characteristics · K-12

## 1 Introduction

With the development of digital educational resource services, the issue of accessibility has been largely resolved, ensuring that all users have the right to access resources (Caiyan, 2022). However, the problem of resource applicability remains inadequately addressed. Resource applicability emphasizes the personalized characteristics of resources to meet the differentiated needs of individuals in resource utilization. To enhance the applicability of resources, existing resource services have begun to leverage data related to users’ learning preferences (Imran et al., 2023), knowledge acquisition states (Duan et al., 2023), learning behaviors (Hernández-de-Menéndez et al., 2022), and learning styles (Troussas et al., 2023) to recommend resources that users require. Nonetheless, most research is based on summaries of practical experiences or theoretical discussions, often overlooking the actual demands of users (Khanal et al., 2020), particularly concerning K-12 teachers for early childhood and grades 1–12 education. This phenomenon results in resource services being insufficient in considering various factors that influence service outcomes, making it challenging for resource services to effectively align with the personalized needs of users.

To enhance the applicability of digital educational resource services, it is necessary to promote a transformation in the service model based on adaptive feedback theory. The exploration of adaptive feedback originated from Thorndike’s law of learning proposed in the early 20th century (Kluger & DeNisi, 1996) and drew inspiration from Skinner’s concepts of positive and negative feedback (Wiliam, 2018), laying the foundation for research on adaptive feedback. With the deepening research on learning feedback in psychology and education, adaptive feedback gradually emerged and continued to be refined. The significant contribution of adaptive feedback theory can be attributed to the publication by Black and Wiliam (1998), who argued that feedback should be based on assessment results and provide appropriate information to enhance learning and teaching for students and teachers. Subsequently, as research progressed in self-regulated learning and other related fields (Jonsson & Panadero, 2018), the theoretical framework of adaptive feedback has been enriched. The integration of adaptive feedback with resource services emphasizes the provision of personalized resources to users through a positive interaction between service supply and users’ demands.

Demand-driven approaches play a crucial role in product and industrial innovation (Frenkel et al., 2015). This study distinguishes itself from previous research based on theoretical discussions (Rozo & Real, 2019) by summarizing construction strategies from a demands perspective to improve the applicability of service outcomes, leading to the design of a three-phase research process (Fig. 1). First, an analytical framework was constructed based on relevant studies. Second, guided by this framework, the TF-IDF (Term Frequency Inverse Document Frequency) text analysis method (Aizawa, 2003) and the Kano model were employed to explore the composition and categories of teachers’ demands for resource services. In the third phase, the characteristics of teachers’ demands were summarized, and construction strategies for resource services were designed based on these demands. Specifically, the literature review informed the design of the analytical framework, the research methodology detailed the samples and data analysis methods, the research results explained the composition, categories, and characteristics of K-12 teachers’ demands, and finally, the research discussion analyzed the construction strategies for resource services. Currently, market forecasts indicate that the market size for adaptive learning systems, which serve as the primary carrier for resource services, is projected to grow from \$2.137 billion in 2024 to \$7.41 billion by 2032 (Dhapte, 2024). Overall, this study not only provides guidance for the development of the resource service market but also supports the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) of equitable and inclusive educational development.

## 2 Literature review

## 2.1 Kano model

The Kano model, proposed by Kano, Seraku, Takahashi and Tsuji in 1984, suggests that there exists a certain linear relationship between the fulfillment of users’ product demands and their satisfaction levels. According to this model, users’ demands can be categorized into five types. Must-be Quality refers to the fundamental expectations users have for a product; failure to meet these demands can lead to dissatisfaction. One-dimensional Quality emphasizes the positive correlation between the degree of demand fulfillment and users’ satisfaction, indicating that higher fulfillment levels correspond to greater satisfaction. Attractive Quality reflects a non-linear relationship between demand fulfillment and satisfaction; when these demands are met, users satisfaction significantly increases, while their absence does not result in dissatisfaction. Indifferent Quality denotes that the fulfillment or lack thereof has no impact on users’ satisfaction. Finally, Reverse Quality indicates that fulfilling these demands may actually decrease users’ satisfaction.

Overall, the Kano model emphasizes that the continuous improvement of product features should be closely related to users’ demands, and its advantages and disadvantages are evident. This model not only helps prioritize product development, but also providing guidance for targeted development. However, the limitations of the Kano model include issues related to the length of the questionnaire design (Matzler et al., 2004), among others. Despite these shortcomings, the Kano model has been widely applied in various fields due to its effective explanation of the relationship between product features and users’ demands. In the field of environmental research, this model can be used to identify factors influencing goal achievement (Dace et al., 2020); in engineering, it can explore users’ perceptions of emerging automotive technologies (Kohli & Singh, 2021).

## 2.2 Adaptive feedback theory

Adaptive feedback focuses on guiding users from their initial level to the desired level by providing personalized feedback. This feedback is provided based on the users’ initial level, current level, and desired level (Beek et al., 2019). The initial level represents the users’ starting point before engaging in the learning activity, while the current level reflects their progress during the learning process. The desired level represents the desired outcome that users aim to achieve through learning. The transition from the initial level to the desired level involves three steps (Fig. 2). Firstly, users receive feedback on learning tasks to assist them in completing those tasks and reaching the desired level. Secondly, upon completion of the learning task, users’ current level is determined. Lastly, as users progress from the current level to the desired level, they receive guidance feedback, which primarily consists of feedback information to direct their learning. Additionally, adjustment feedback is provided based on users’ emotion, learning motivation, and other factors. This adjustment feedback helps regulate their internal emotional state and ensures a sustained high level of motivation throughout the learning process.

Figure 3 illustrates the detailed procedure through which adaptive feedback is delivered. Firstly, a suitable learning task is offered to the users based on their prior knowledge (Kluger & DeNisi, 1996). Secondly, formative and summative evaluations are conducted as users progress through the learning task. These evaluations continuously monitor the users’ internal and external learning states in real time (Narciss & Huth, 2004). Finally, based on the evaluation results and collected data, a judg ment is made regarding the need for new learning task feedback, guidance feedback, or adjustment feedback (Nicol & Macfarlane-Dick, 2006). This assistance aims to facilitate users in completing the learning task and achieving the transition from the initial level to the desired level. Moreover, adaptive feedback places emphasis on optimizing feedback by considering the results of the users’ experience (Ouyang et al., 2019).

The principles of adaptive feedback provide a clear framework that outlines the essential elements required for its implementation. These elements include level gap diagnosis strategies, feedback information, learning contexts, users’ characteristics, and technical support. Together, they emphasize the importance of considering the gap between the initial level and the desired level, the situational state, and the users characteristics to provide personalized feedback using technology. The diagnostic strategy is a fundamental component of adaptive feedback as it determines the users initial level, desired level, and the gap between them (Ramaprasad, 1983). The feedback information consists of three aspects: feedback content, feedback presentation, and feedback function. The element ensure that the feedback provided is comprehensive and effective. The learning situation include learning objectives, among other factors, which help tailor feedback to the specific learning context. The users characteristics element include prior knowledge, learning motivation, among others (Narciss & Huth, 2004). The element enables the feedback to be personalized according to the users’ unique needs. Additionally, technical support focuses on utilizing learning analysis technology to diagnose the users’ real-time status, such as learning analysis dashboards (Verbert et al., 2014) and concept maps (Kroeze et al., 2021).

In summary, feedback information, users’ status, and technical conditions are the core components of adaptive feedback. Feedback information refers to the information that assists users in learning knowledge, and it can be categorized into various types based on different criteria. Based on the form of feedback information, it can be classified as positive feedback and negative feedback (Sarkany & Deitte, 2017). Additionally, feedback can be distinguished based on its external form, such as users interaction feedback (Hinojosa, 2022) or peers’ interaction feedback (Liu & Lin, 2007). The users’ status encompasses the users’ status before, during, and after learning, and it can be analyzed from three aspects: cognition, emotion, and physical (Sardar et al., 2022). Technical support includes the agents responsible for implementing adaptive feedback and the employment of learning analytics technology to diagnose the users’ status. This technology aids in gathering and analyzing data to better understand the users’ learning progress and inform the feedback provided.

## 2.3 Digital educational resource services

In research related to the construction of resource services, scholars generally agree that the development of resource services should be approached from multiple perspectives, with key aspects including digital educational resources, platforms, technological integration, and infrastructure environments. Specifically, digital educational resources should possess objectivity, effectively integrate with teaching activities, and have broad coverage (Xie et al., 2018). The platform should be easily accessible and offer diverse functionalities (Haleem et al., 2022). Technological integration and infrastructure environmental factors should ensure the timeliness of services and align with the needs of users (Hehir et al., 2021). Based on this analysis, this study posits that the focus of resource services construction should concentrate on the development of foundational environments and technological advancements.

When constructing digital educational resource services, several fundamental aspects require attention. These include resource development, resource sharing, service platform construction, and service environment construction. In resource development, the primary objective is to meet the resource requirements of users. This entails diversifying the types of available resources (Kuhlmann et al., 2023), aligning them with users’ digital capabilities (Ervianti et al., 2023), ensuring an adequate quantity of resources (Leshchenko et al., 2021), and maintaining consistency with teaching and learning activities (Xie et al., 2018). By adopting this approach, the needs of various learning styles and competency levels can be accommodated, comprehensively addressing all needs and catering to multiple scenarios. Resource sharing aims to enhance both the quantity and variety of available resources, ultimately improving resource quality. Facilitating the sharing of resources can expand the range of options for users, enriching their learning experiences (Liu et al., 2021). The service platform plays a crucial role in facilitating users’ learning and serves as a medium for resource services (Decuypere et al., 2021). It acts as a powerful tool that enables users to access and utilize resources effectively, enhancing their overall learning experience. The construction of the service environment focuses on creating an intelligent teaching and learning environment (Cheung et al., 2021). This environment is designed to diagnose users’ status and provide resource services. By harnessing cutting-edge technologies like artificial intelligence and data analytics, the capability to personalize the learning experience and customize resource services to cater to the unique requirements of individual users is achievable.

When ensuring application reliability, focusing on the integration of artificial intelligence technology, specifically in the construction of users’ status diagnosis and resource recommendation algorithms, becomes essential. Numerous users’ status diagnosis and resource recommendation algorithms have been developed in relevant research. To facilitate resource recommendations for users, an analysis is conducted on their status. For instance, Yuanfei (2022) utilizes a convolutional neural network to recognize users’ online behavior and make resource recommendations based on the findings. To address the issue of the system’s lack of information about new users and its struggle to provide accurate resource recommendations, Chen and Deng (2021) propose a method to recommend required resources based on the analysis of the resources that other users have already learned. Resource recommendations based on cognitive analysis rely heavily on knowledge graphs. In related studies, Wan and Yu (2023) predict the learning outcomes of target knowledge points based on users\` understanding of different knowledge and the relationships between them. This approach allows for the creation of personalized learning paths and the provision of appropriate resources to users. Resource recommendations based on social networks focus on the relationships between users. Gómez-García et al. (2023) suggest that there is a correlation between social networks and users’ resource needs and propose a strategy that utilizes users’ social networks to cluster users and recommend resources.

The research conducted on digital educational resource services emphasizes the importance of resources, platforms, algorithms, and intelligent environments in the development and quality of these services. These elements play crucial roles in ensuring effective resource services. Resources are the fundamental support for service development, and they have specific requirements in terms of content, type, quantity, ease of use, and alignment with service scenarios. They provide the necessary information for users to engage in effective learning experiences. The platform serves as the medium for sharing, integrating, and delivering resource services to users. By facilitating seamless access and utilization of resources, users can benefit from a wide variety of educational materials available. Algorithms are at the core of users\` status diagnosis and personalized resource recommendations. They require a multi-dimensional diagnosis of users’ status and aim to provide users with resources that accurately meet their needs. These algorithms enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of resource services. The intelligent environment encompasses the essential hardware for service development, which includes users’ digital devices and the environment that can continually perceive users’ status in real time.

An extensive examination of research on digital educational resource services and adaptive feedback reveals that the construction of resource services requires attention to four key aspects: resources, platform, algorithms, and infrastructure (Table 1).

**Table 1** Components of resource services

| Aspect | Dimension |
| --- | --- |
| Resources | Content Relevance Variety of Types Quantity Adequacy Ease of Use Process Fit |
| Platform | Resource Sharing Resource Integration Users' Feedback Channel Respond to Users' Demands |
| Algorithms | Accuracy of Results Accurate Identification of Status Flexible and Diverse |
| Infrastructure | Personal Digital Devices Intelligent Environment |

These aspects encompass various considerations that contribute to the effectiveness of resource services. As feedback information, resources should ensure the relevance of content and knowledge, diversity of types or formats, coverage of users’ needs, appropriate difficulty for users’ digital capabilities, and suitability for the teaching process. The platform, as a technical condition, plays a crucial role in facilitating resource services. It should enable efficient sharing of resources, seamless integration of different resources, effective feedback on the service experience from users, and quick responsiveness to the demands of users. Algorithms, as the foundation for diagnosing technical conditions and users’ status, are vital in achieving accurate resource recommendations. They should ensure the precision of recommendation results, accurately identify users’ status, and promptly respond to users’ needs based on their status. Infrastructure, as a technical condition, needs support from personal digital devices and intelligent environments.

## 3 Methodology

## 3.1 Data collection

In this study, data collection was carried out through interviews and questionnaires. Structured interviews were conducted to gain insights into K-12 teachers’ demands for resource services, which used the components of resource services as the framework for the interviews. The interviewees were K-12 teachers, and the interview questions covered four key aspects: resources, platform, algorithms, and infrastructure (Table 2). Furthermore, the questionnaire method combined with the Kano model to explore K-12 teachers’ attitudes towards each demand for resource services. This approach allowed for classification of these demands based on the level of satisfaction they elicited. By utilizing the Kano model, the significance and impact of each demand were assessed, which provided a comprehensive understanding of teachers preferences and priorities regarding resource services.

## 3.2 Data analysis

This study aimed to comprehensively analyze K-12 teachers’ demands for resource services and addressed the shortcomings of previous demand analyses that overlooked the authenticity of these demands, based on a constructed analytical framework. To achieve this, the study first employed the TF-IDF text analysis method to extract main sentences from each interview question related to the demands, thereby quickly understanding teachers’ responses, verifying the existence of the demands, and exploring the underlying reasons for these demands. Subsequently, the Kano model was utilized for data analysis to classify teachers’ demands and determine the priorities for meeting these demands. Additionally, the application of TF-IDF in text analysis demonstrated high credibility, with relevant studies successfully applying it in areas such as news content detection (Gupta & Meel, 2021), social content prediction (Lubis et al., 2021), and webpage content summarization (Manjari et al., 2020).

The TF-IDF text analysis method extracts the main sentences by evaluating the importance of words in the text. Its fundamental concept is that the higher the frequency of a word’s occurrence in the text, the greater its significance to the semantic meaning of the text. The assessment of word importance is determined by the TF-IDF value. To calculate the TF-IDF value of a word, one must first calculate the TF and IDF values; TF (Term Frequency) is the ratio of the frequency of a specific word in the text to the total number of words in the text, while IDF (Inverse Document Frequency) reflects the generality of a word across the entire corpus. Its calculation formula is presented in Eq. 1, where N is the total number of documents in the text and $d f _ { t }$ is the number of documents containing that word. The TF-IDF value is the product of the TF and IDF values (Aizawa, 2003). In practical application, the first step in this study was to preprocess the interview content text by removing function words; the second step was to calculate the TF-IDF value for each word based on tokenization; the third step was to extract keywords based on the calculation results and analyze the context of each keyword; the fourth step was to design the main sentence for each demand interview text based on the results of the contextual analysis.

Equation 1 Formula for calculating IDF.

$$
I D F = \log \left(\frac {N}{d f _ {t}}\right)\tag{1}
$$

The Kano model classifies demands based on the Better and Worse coefficients. The calculation of these two coefficients is based on whether a particular demand is present or absent in users’ responses. By analyzing the responses to both positive and negative questions regarding the same demand, the corresponding types of demand can be identified as follows: A (Attractive Quality), O (One-dimensional Quality), M (Must-be Quality), I (Indifferent Quality), and R (Reverse Quality). Subsequently, the respective formulas are used to calculate the Better and Worse coefficients (Eq. 2). Each demand’s two coefficients are then plotted as X and Y values in a two-dimensional coordinate system, with the Better coefficient as the vertical axis and the Worse coefficient as the horizontal axis. Finally, based on the averages of Better and Worse coefficients, the coordinate system is divided into four quadrants, thereby determin ing the type corresponding to each demand (Meng, 2022). In this study, a questionnaire containing both positive and negative demand questions was first designed, and then the Better and Worse coefficients for each demand were calculated based on the questionnaire results. Lastly, the classification results for each demand were derived based on their positions in the coordinate system.

Equation 2 Calculation formula for Better and Worse coefficients.

$$
\begin{array}{c} B e t t e r = \frac {A + O}{A + O + M + I} \\ W o r s e = - \frac {O + M}{A + O + M + I} \end{array}\tag{2}
$$

## 3.3 Data sources

This study employed a stratified sampling method to select interview subjects and to distribute questionnaires. The level of digital construction in education has a significant impact on the implementation of teaching activities (Begicevic Redjep et al., 2021) and also affects teachers’ demands for educational resource services. In China, due to differences in economic development, there are significant disparities in the level of digital construction across different regions, particularly between eastern, central, and western areas, as well as between rural and urban schools. To comprehensively collect demand data from teachers in different regions, this study used a stratified sampling method. This approach ensured that the interview subjects and questionnaire recipients represented various geographical areas and different types of schools.

Regarding the interview data, this study conducted interviews with 56 teachers across the eastern, central, and western regions of China (Table 3). The sample included both urban and rural schools, encompassing nine different subjects.

In terms of questionnaire data sources, the survey conducted using the Kano model took the form of questionnaires. A total of 1,000 questionnaires were distributed, and 964 were successfully retrieved. Among the 964 K-12 teachers who completed the questionnaire, 452 were from the eastern region, 388 from the central region, 124 from the western region, with 716 from rural schools and 248 from urban schools (Table 4).

## 4 Results

## 4.1 Composition of resource services demand

In this section, the study conducted a TF-IDF analysis on the interview texts for each demand to extract words that significantly influenced the semantics. Based on the context of these words, the main sentences of each demand’s interview text were summarized, providing a detailed description of the demands.

The results of the text analysis regarding digital educational resources (Table 5) indicate that teachers require resources that can be efficiently integrated into teaching activities. Specific demands include: first, the content of the resources should not only relate to the teaching material but also match the personal learning abilities and knowledge foundations of both teachers and students; second, the types of resources should encompass static display resources, dynamic resources, and interactive resources; third, the quantity of resources must meet the demands of various scenarios, including teaching, professional development, and students’ self-regulated learning; fourth, the application difficulty of the resources should align with the digital capabilities of teachers and students; finally, the resources should be compatible with various instructional models, such as problem-based learning and collaborative learning, to better integrate into teaching activities.

The results of the text analysis regarding the platform (Table 6) reveal that teachers hope to enhance the openness of the platform. Specific demands include: first, the establishment of seamless resource-sharing channels to eliminate barriers in resource sharing between teachers and students; second, the platform should possess cross-platform resource integration capabilities, which would not only enrich the resource system of the platform but also facilitate the search for needed resources by teachers and students; third, the platform should provide multiple feedback channels for various requests, exploring new feedback methods such as phone calls and emails in addition to comments and ratings; finally, the platform should be able to respond quickly to feedback from teachers and students, timely meeting their new demands.

The results of the text analysis regarding algorithms (Table 7) indicate that teachers’ overall demands for algorithms are to comprehensively diagnose the status of teachers and students and provide resources that meet their needs. Specific demands include: first, the algorithm should have diagnostic functions for physical and emotional states, breaking through the limitations of relying solely on cognitive state to achieve a comprehensive assessment of the status of teachers and students; second, it should be capable of providing personalized resources for scenarios such as professional development and students’ self-regulated learning; third, it should be able to flexibly adjust service strategies based on real-time changes in the status, learning styles, resource requirements, and learning activities of teachers and students, thereby meeting their personalized needs.

## 4.2 Classification of resource services demand

The Kano model data analysis results for teachers’ resource service demands indicated that these demands could be categorized into Attractive Quality, One-dimensional Quality, and Indifferent Quality. To classify teachers’ demands, this study first calculated the Better and Worse coefficients for each demand to explore the impact of the fulfillment level of different demands on teacher satisfaction (Table 9). Next, the mean values of the Better and Worse coefficients for all demands were calculated, and based on this, a two-dimensional coordinate system was constructed with four quadrants. Finally, each demand was marked in the two-dimensional coordinate system according to its Better and Worse coefficients (Fig. 4), and the results showed that the demands could be divided into three types (Table 10).

Attractive Quality refers to the demands that teachers believe should be met by resource services, including convenient access to services and resource acquisition, as well as personalized resource recommendations tailored to teaching scenario. Convenient access to services first requires the capability of resource services to operate across platforms, including hardware such as computers, tablets, and smartphones, as well as operating systems such as Windows, Mac, Android, and iOS. Additionally, the dependence of resource services on low-cost intelligent environments is also important, requiring them to operate within existing environments. For convenient resource acquisition, platforms need to provide effective channels for resource sharing among teachers and students from different regions. Furthermore, platforms must have strong resource integration capabilities to facilitate resource retrieval for teachers and students. Personalized resource recommendations tailored to teaching scenario require platforms to design flexible recommendation strategies that consider the characteristics of teaching scenario and other factors.

Performance Quality pertains to the demands that teachers hope resource services will fulfill, including comprehensive status diagnosis, higher quality resources, and personalized resource recommendations for professional development and students’ self-regulated learning. Due to limitations in teacher capacity, it is challenging to supervise and diagnose the status of all students. Therefore, teachers hope that resource services can provide comprehensive status diagnosis from physical and emotional dimensions, offering a basis for personalized teaching activities. Higher quality resources, on one hand, require expanding the coverage of resources, including those for teacher professional development and those needed for students’ self-regulated learning. Additionally, it is necessary to enrich the types of resources to accommodate the diverse learning styles of teachers and students. The demand for expanding resource recommendations indicates that teachers hope the platform can provide recommendations not only for teaching scenario but also for professional development and students’ self-regulated learning. To achieve this, it is essential to design flexible service models that integrate the characteristics of different scenarios.

Indifferent Quality consists of demands that have little impact on teachers’ satisfaction with resource services. Indifferent Quality refers to characteristics that teachers perceive as optional in resource services. The reason teachers consider ease of use, content relevance, process fit, and cognitive state diagnosis as unimportant is that these demands are already being met by existing resource services. Firstly, the current resource services are based on curriculum standards, ensuring the connection between resource content and teaching content, as well as the adaptability of resources to teaching activities. Moreover, the resources primarily consist of PowerPoints and videos, which require low digital capability from teachers, ensuring simplicity and ease of use. Secondly, although the existing resource services provide limited cognitive diagnosis results, they still facilitate personalized teaching to a certain extent. Additionally, teachers consider feedback channels and responsiveness to be unimportant because these demands appear to have no direct impact on teaching effectiveness. In reality, this is because teachers have become accustomed to passively accepting the existing resource services and have not realized the role their own demands play in improving the services.

## 4.3 Characteristics of resource services demand

From a horizontal perspective, the demands of K-12 teachers for resource services exhibit characteristics of convenience and diversity. Convenience refers to teachers requirements for access to services and quality resources. They expect resource services to reduce dependence on intelligent environments and ensure that both teachers and students can access resources at minimal cost. Additionally, teachers hope that resource services can establish a vast resource system through enhanced platform integration capabilities or by providing effective channels for resource sharing among teachers and students. Furthermore, resources need to remain connected with the ever-changing needs of teachers and students, efficiently enriching the resource library and promptly responding to their requirements. Diversity pertains to the requirements for resource service scenarios, necessitating personalized resource recommendations for teaching, professional development, and students’ self-regulated learning. This assists in facilitating personalized teaching activities and continuously improving resource services based on feedback from teachers and students.

From a vertical perspective, the demands of K-12 teachers for resource services exhibit characteristics of stages and evolution. Stages refer to the requirements for service scenario development, with teachers prioritizing the needs of teaching scenario as the most important, followed by professional development and students self-regulated learning scenarios. Evolution refers to the developmental requirements for resource service elements. In terms of resource development, synchronization with service scenarios development is prioritized, continuously expanding the coverage of resources. Basic demands of teachers and students regarding resource content are given precedence, followed by the enrichment of resource types and improved usability. Platform development requires continuous improvement of resource integration and sharing capabilities, as well as the ability to quickly respond to the demands of teachers and students. Regarding the algorithm aspect, the design of the status diagnosis algorithm should first enhance the capability for diagnosing cognitive state, assessing the cognitive state of teachers and students from multiple perspectives, and then meet the requirements for diagnosing physical and emotional states. Additionally, the design of the recommendation algorithm focuses on continuously enhancing the comprehensive analysis capabilities of various factors. Infrastructure development requires the synchronization of service development with the construction of intelligent environments, gradually increasing the requirements for these environments.

## 5 Discussion and implication

This study conducted further interviews to explore the reasons behind K-12 teachers’ various demands for resource services in depth, ultimately discovering that the discussion should focus on two aspects: the composition of demands and their prioritization. In terms of demand composition, an analysis of the interview content revealed that usability, ease of use, and infrastructure are the three main factors driving teachers’ demands, which aligns with the findings of Scherer et al. (2019). In resource services, the ineffective integration of resource development and technology application into actual teaching diminishes the usefulness of the services; low teacher participation in service development and insufficient collaboration between different platforms further affect the ease of use of the services. Additionally, the quality of infrastructure declines due to insufficient funding in various schools. In summary, teachers require support from resource services in their teaching, but the aforementioned factors reduce teachers experience of these services, leading to diverse demands for the construction of resource services. Regarding the prioritization of demand fulfillment, it is primarily influenced by teachers’ work responsibilities. Therefore, the first priority is to provide personalized services for classroom teaching scenario, followed by personalized resource services for professional development and students’ self-regulated learning. This order of demands largely aligns with the evolution of educational informatization, which expands from teaching scenario to other contexts, as well as the concept of prioritizing student development in teachers professional ethics (Kretz, 2014).

Based on the Kano model and adaptive feedback theory, this study analyzes the requirements of K-12 teachers for the construction of resource services. Theoretically, this research not only integrates studies on resource quality (Apoki et al., 2019), resource recommendation (da Silva et al., 2023), and adaptive learning systems (Peng et al., 2019), but also promotes further development in these fields. Firstly, it highlights that resource construction should consider not only the content of the resources and their integration into teaching but also the alignment of resources with the digital capabilities of both teachers and students. Secondly, precise resource recommendations should leverage learner portraits, contextual and resource characteristics. Learner portraits should encompass not only the cognitive state of teachers and students but also their physical and emotional states. Contextual characteristics should include information such as teaching objectives and instructional phases, while resource characteristics should address the difficulty and detail of the resources. Finally, this study enriches the conceptual framework of adaptive learning systems by emphasizing the importance of information such as learner portraits, learning data, and user feedback.

From a practical perspective, this research posits that the construction of resource services should follow a phased approach. The first phase should focus on advancing relevant constructions around teaching scenario: firstly, resources that meet the demands of teaching scenario should be developed; secondly, the platform’s capability for resource integration and sharing should be enhanced, along with the provision of feedback channels such as comments and ratings; thirdly, algorithms capable of diagnosing students’ cognitive state should be designed; and fourthly, the cross-platform operational capacity of services should be improved based on existing devices and classroom environments. The second phase of service development should concentrate on providing effective professional development services as well as supporting students’ self-regulated learning, further advancing related elements: firstly, it should prioritize meeting the resource demands of professional development and students’ self-regulated learning scenarios; secondly, it should develop integration and sharing capabilities tailored to new scenarios, actively exploring new feedback channels such as phone and email; thirdly, it should design algorithms for diagnosing teachers’ cognitive state; and fourthly, it should continue to enhance the cross-platform operational capacity of services based on existing devices and infrastructure. The third phase of service development should center on quality enhancement, promoting the sustainable development of services: firstly, it should emphasize the diversity and usability of resources; secondly, it should explore more effective models for resource integration and sharing; thirdly, it should design algorithms for diagnosing the physical and emotional states of teachers and students; and fourthly, it should develop higher-performance functionalities to positively contribute to the construction of intelligent environments.

## 6 Conclusion

This study, guided by the theory of adaptive feedback and incorporating interview methods, TF-IDF text analysis algorithms, and the Kano model, explores the composition, categories, and characteristics of K-12 teachers’ needs for resource services. This provides important guidance for the construction of resource services and outlines trends and tasks for building effective resource services in a phased manner. However, this study also has some limitations. First, the scope of respondents and survey subjects is relatively limited, primarily focusing on K-12 schools and not adequately considering the demands of higher education. Second, the research emphasizes teachers’ demands while neglecting those of students. Lastly, it does not propose specific strategies for implementing each demand. Future research should further expand the participant scope to effectively explore the demands of both teachers and students for resource services and design specific strategies that address each demand from a technological perspective.

**Data availability** The questionnaire data used for classifying and analyzing the digital educational resource service demands of K-12 teachers based on the Kano model in this study is available for public access and can be obtained from the corresponding author. However, the interview data of K-12 teachers are subject to a confidentiality agreement established between the researchers and the participants, and therefore, specific details of the interview content cannot be disclosed.
